**Ch 021 draft analysis:**

- "If there was a hostess who had a right to consider herself fashionable as well as charming, it was Lady Margaret Beaumont; yet one morning at breakfast there..." — The source said "If there was in those days a country house in England which had a right to call itself broad in views and large in tastes, it was Bretton in Yorkshire; and if there was a hostess..." The draft dropped the Bretton/Yorkshire half of the parallel structure. "There" now has no antecedent — breakfast where? The reader has no idea where "there" refers to, since "Bretton" and "Yorkshire" were cut. This is a genuine dangling reference.

- "He saw a score of societies which seemed quite independent of each other—the smartest was the smallest, almost wholly strange to him; the largest was the sporting world, also unknown." — Parses fine; the ellipsis of explanation is just compression.

- "One morning, April 27, 1863, he was asked to breakfast with the old Court physician who had been friendly with the Legation in the teeth of society." — Sir Henry Holland is authorized-cut (he's on the minor-character removal list). This is an authorized-cut residue; not a finding.

**Ch 022 draft analysis:**

- "Again one went to meditate on the steps of the Santa Maria in Ara Cœli, but the lesson seemed as shallow as before." — "Again" implies a prior visit to this same place. In the draft, there is no prior mention of the Santa Maria in Ara Cœli or of meditating there. The source establishes the first visit earlier in the same chapter, but that passage was NOT cut — wait, let me re-read the source. The source in Ch 022 says "Again one went to meditate on the steps of the Santa Maria in Ara Cœli" — and this "again" refers back to Ch 019/020 source material (the earlier Rome visit), not to anything in Ch 022. Checking the draft of Ch 021 — there is no mention of the Santa Maria in Ara Cœli there either. The draft of Ch 022 itself has no prior mention of it. So "again" and "as shallow as before" are both dangling — there is no antecedent visit in any preceding draft. However, this same "again" is present in the source of Ch 022, meaning the source itself references a prior chapter's event. The question is whether the prior chapter draft established it. The Ch 021 draft does not mention the Santa Maria in Ara Cœli at all. The source for this cross-reference would be in much earlier chapters (Rome sections). This is ambiguous — it may be an authorized subplot removal residue from earlier chapters. I'll set this aside as it's a cross-chapter reference beyond the pair scope.

- "He was a dramatist; a painter; a poet, like Carlyle." — The antecedent "he" here refers to Macaulay, but Macaulay was last named two sentences back: "Macaulay was the English historian... anyone who should even distantly imitate Macaulay would perish in self-contempt. One might as well imitate Shakespeare. He was a dramatist..." — "He" here could be read as Shakespeare (the immediately preceding noun) rather than Macaulay, which is who the source means. This is a genuine dangling/ambiguous pronoun. A competent reader would genuinely be confused about whether "he" means Shakespeare or Macaulay.

- "One morning Palgrave took him to Sotheby's, where, among a portfolio of old drawings, he marked a sheet attributed to Rafael for a bid: 'It looks to me like one of those things that sell for five shillings one day, and fifty pounds the next.'" — The quoted speech is Palgrave's in the source ("I should buy this," he said; "it looks to me like..."). The draft's compression makes it read as though either Adams or Palgrave marked the sheet and spoke the words, but the quotation is unattributed — the grammatical subject of "he marked" is ambiguous (could be Adams or Palgrave), and the dialogue is presented without clear speaker attribution. However, in context "he marked" most naturally reads as Adams following Palgrave's advice, and the quotation in context reads as Palgrave's words. A competent reader would likely understand this as Palgrave speaking. This is borderline — I'll apply the gate test strictly: the reader is slightly confused about who marked the sheet and who spoke, but can infer Palgrave spoke. Not a clear finding.

- "Frank Palgrave, unable to work off his restlessness in travel, became a critic." — "Unable to work off his restlessness in travel" implies a contrast with someone who did work it off in travel. The source says "unable to work off his restlessness in travel like Gifford." Gifford (Gifford Palgrave) was an authorized-cut minor character. The phrase now dangles without the comparison. But does this pass the gate test? A reader would read "unable to work off his restlessness in travel" as simply a personal characteristic explaining why he became a critic — slightly odd but parseable. Marginally not a genuine confusion.

Now back to the Ch 021 finding about "breakfast there":

The source: "If there was in those days a country house in England which had a right to call itself broad in views and large in tastes, it was Bretton in Yorkshire; and if there was a hostess who had a right to consider herself fashionable as well as charming, it was Lady Margaret Beaumont; yet one morning at breakfast there, sitting by her side..."

The draft: "If there was a hostess who had a right to consider herself fashionable as well as charming, it was Lady Margaret Beaumont; yet one morning at breakfast there, sitting by her side..."

"There" = Bretton. Bretton is entirely absent from the draft. A reader has no idea where "breakfast there" is. This is a genuine dangling demonstrative.

The Macaulay/Shakespeare "he" finding: In the draft, "One might as well imitate Shakespeare. He was a dramatist; a painter; a poet, like Carlyle." The immediately preceding grammatical subject is Shakespeare, so "he" reads as Shakespeare. But the source makes clear this refers to Macaulay. A competent reader would genuinely be misled into thinking this describes Shakespeare.
